title: The History of Dynamite — The Explosive That Built the Modern World
fullText: In 1888, a Swedish chemist opened his morning newspaper in Paris [music] and found something no living person should ever have to read, his own obituary. A French reporter had mixed up Alfred Nobel with his brother Ludvig, who had actually died [music] while vacationing in Can. The newspaper did not hold back. It called [music] Nobel, the merchant of death. It said he had become rich by finding ways to kill more people faster than ever before. Alfred Nobel sat there reading those words, realizing that this was exactly how the entire world was going to remember him. But what nobody knew at the time was that Nobel had never intended his invention for warfare. He created dynamite to save the lives of construction workers and miners who were being blown apart by unstable nitroglycerin on a daily basis. And that obituary, [music] that brutal, premature summary of his life, would haunt him so deeply that he would eventually give away almost his entire fortune to create the most prestigious awards in human history. This is the story of dynamite, the invention that built the modern world and nearly destroyed the reputation of the man who made it. Stockholm, Sweden, 1833. Alfred Bernhard Nobel came into the world as the third son of Emanuel and Andreette Nobel and the family had almost nothing. Emmanuel was an inventor and engineer with big ideas [music] but terrible luck. The couple had eight children and only four of them survived past childhood. Stockholm in the 1830s was not kind to struggling [music] families and the Nobels were barely getting by. But Emanuel Nobel was a stubborn man. He packed up his family and moved them to St. Petersburg, Russia, where he had landed a contract with the Russian military. Suddenly, the broke inventor from Stockholm was manufacturing explosive sea mines and torpedoes for the Tsar Navy. The factory boomed during the Crimean War in the 1850s. And for the first time in Alfred's life, the family had real money. Private tutors [music] replaced public schooling. Alfred became fluent in Swedish, Russian, English, French, and German by the time he was a teenager. The kid was brilliant, particularly in chemistry. Though what he really [music] wanted to do was write poetry. His father was not interested in raising a poet. At 16, Emmanuel sent [music] Alfred to Paris to study chemistry under a professor named Theophile Jules Paloo. It was inside that Parisian laboratory where young Alfred Nobel first encountered the substance that would define his entire life. Working alongside [music] him was an Italian chemist named Ascanio Sbrero, the man who had first [music] synthesized nitroglycerin back in 1846. Nitroglycerin was in simple [music] terms an absolute monster of a chemical. It was roughly 10 times more powerful than gunpowder. A small vial of it could blast through solid rock. But it had one massive problem. [music] It was wildly, horrifyingly unstable. A bump, a temperature change, sometimes seemingly nothing at all, and it would [music] detonate without warning. So himself was so disturbed by what he had created that he actively warned people against [music] using it. He called it too dangerous to be of any practical use. Alfred Nobel looked at that same substance and saw opportunity, not because he wanted to build weapons, because he understood that the world desperately needed a better explosive for construction and mining. Workers were dying in mines and railroad tunnels [music] every single day using black powder, the only real option available at the time. Black powder was weak, unreliable, and painfully slow. Nitroglycerin could do the job a 100 times better if only someone could figure out how to handle it without getting killed in the process. After Paris, Nobel [music] spent time in the United States apprenticing under the Swedish American inventor John Ericson. He eventually returned to St. Petersburg to work in his father's munitions factory. But when the Crimean War ended in 1856, the Russian military [music] contracts dried up and the Nobel family business went bankrupt. The family moved back to Sweden, humbled and broke once again. This is where Alfred's obsession with nitroglycerin kicked into high gear. He and his father began experimenting with ways to manufacture and detonate it safely. In 1863, Alfred made his first major breakthrough, the blasting [music] cap. This was a small device that used a controlled shock rather than heat to detonate nitroglycerin. Before this, setting off nitroglycerin was essentially a game of chance. The blasting cap changed that. For the first time, you could trigger an explosion precisely when and where you wanted it. The Nobel company built its first nitroglycerin factory in 1865 [music] outside Stockholm, and business started moving fast. Then came September 3rd, 1864. An explosion ripped through the [music] Nobel family's factory at Helenorg. The blast killed five people, including Alfred's youngest brother, Emile, who was just 21 years old. The details were devastating. The workshop was completely destroyed. [music] Emile was gone. Alfred's father, Emanuel, suffered a stroke shortly afterward and never fully recovered. The Swedish government revoked Alfred's license to produce explosives inside Stockholm city limits. Neighbors wanted nothing to do with the Nobels. Alfred was treated like a menace. But Alfred Nobel did not stop. He moved his operation to a barge anchored on a lake outside the city where he could work in isolation without endangering anyone [music] nearby. He later established a new factory at a place called Vintican. The death of his brother did not push him away from explosives. [music] It pulled him deeper in because the problem was clear. Nitroglycerin in its liquid form was too [music] dangerous for anyone to use safely. Someone had to fix that. And Nobel decided that someone was going to be him. And the world needed that fix more urgently than most people realized because nitroglycerin was already being used in construction projects and it was killing people at an alarming rate. In April of 1866, 70 crates of nitroglycerin exploded aboard a steam ship called the European while it was docked in Aspenwall, [music] Panama. 50 people were killed instantly. 2 weeks later, a crate of nitroglycerin that had been shipped across the ISMAS detonated inside a Wells Fargo office on Montgomery [music] Street in San Francisco. The blast leveled the building and killed 15 people. A Wells Fargo employee had been trying to open the leaking crate with a hammer and chisel. 2 days after that, six more workers died along the Central Pacific Railroad line in the Sierra Nevada mountains while transporting nitroglycerin [music] to a tunnel construction site. California immediately banned the transportation of liquid nitroglycerin across the entire state. These were not isolated incidents. Nitroglycerin explosions were happening everywhere from factory floors in Europe [music] to mining camps in the American West. The substance was simply too volatile in its pure liquid state. Any vibration, any [music] shock, any shift in temperature could set it off. Workers called it blasting oil, and they used it anyway because nothing else came close to its power. The problem was that it frequently did not work the way anyone intended. Nobel spent years testing different combinations, trying to find a material that could absorb [music] nitroglycerin and make it stable enough to handle and transport without [music] spontaneous detonation. He tried sawdust, charcoal, cement, and dozens of other substances. [music] Nothing worked well enough. Then he discovered kieselgur, a type [music] of fine chalky sedimentary rock, also known as dietimmacous earth made from the fossilized remains of tiny [music] ancient sea creatures. It had an incredible ability to soak up liquids. When Nobel [music] mixed nitroglycerin into kaselgur, the result was a soft moldable paste that could be shaped into sticks, wrapped in paper, and handled without blowing up. You could [music] drop it, ship it across an ocean, store it in a warehouse, and it would just sit there completely inert until [music] you triggered it with a blasting cap. Nobel patented this invention in 1867. He called it dynamite from the Greek word dynamis, meaning power. And the name was fitting because dynamite was not just a safer version of nitroglycerin. It was a completely [music] new category of tool. It was portable, reliable, and roughly 10 times more powerful than gunpowder. You could drill holes into solid rock, insert a stick of dynamite, attach a blasting cap [music] and a fuse, and blast outward in a controlled direction. This was not [music] just a massive increase in explosive force. It fundamentally changed the geometry of demolition. Instead of a chaotic, unpredictable explosion that scattered debris [music] everywhere, dynamite directed the blast outward from the drill hole, shattering [music] rock exactly where you needed it to shatter. Nobel patented dynamite in the United States and the United Kingdom, and then set out to sell it to the entire world. He traveled [music] across Britain with a suitcase literally filled with dynamite, arranging demonstrations in mining [music] districts and inviting the press to watch him blast rock formations apart. Within a decade, Nobel had established 16 explosives factories across 14 [music] countries. He was selling dynamite to mining companies, railroad [music] builders, canal engineers, and construction firms on every continent. The DuPont [music] Company in the United States became one of his chief partners. Nobel was becoming [music] extraordinarily wealthy and he was still in his 30s. By 1875, Nobel [music] had already improved on his own invention, creating blasting gelatin, which was even more stable and [music] more powerful than standard dynamite. 12 years after that, he patented ballastite, a nearly smokeless powder that would become a precursor to modern military propellants. Nobel held 355 patents over the course of his [music] lifetime, but dynamite remained his masterpiece, and its impact on the physical world was about to become staggering. The scale of what dynamite made possible is almost hard to wrap your head around. Before 1867, construction crews relied on black powder and raw manual labor to cut through mountains and dig tunnels. Black powder had been the standard for centuries, and it was painfully slow. You could blast small sections of rock, sure, but major geological obstacles could take years to penetrate. Dynamite changed that equation overnight. Take the American Transcontinental Railroad. The Central Pacific Railroad was trying to push its tracks through the Sierra Nevada mountains in California during the 1860s, and the biggest [music] obstacle in its path was the Summit Tunnel, a passage that had to be carved through solid granite at the highest point of the mountain range. Workers using black powder were making progress of barely more than 1 ft per day. The granite was so hard and so dense that conventional blasting powder could barely scratch it. When they switched to nitroglycerin and later dynamite, [music] the rate of excavation nearly doubled. In some sections at the bottom of the tunnel, [music] progress jumped from 2 and 1/2 ft per day to over 4 ft per day. That does not sound like much, but when you are boring [music] through the spine of a mountain range, every inch matters. The summit tunnel took years, even with explosives. Without them, it might never have been finished at all. But the transcontinental railroad was just the beginning. The real proving ground for dynamite was [music] the Panama Canal. One of the most ambitious and brutal engineering projects in human history. The idea was simple enough on a map Carter channeled across the narrow isithmas of Panama to connect [music] the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. The reality was something else entirely. The terrain was mountainous jungle with an average temperature of 80° and over 100 in of rainfall per [music] year. Tropical diseases killed workers by the thousands. Landslides buried equipment and swallowed entire work sites. [music] And at the center of it all was the CBRA cut, an artificial valley that had to be carved through the continental divide itself. 6,000 [music] men worked the Calbra cut at any given time, drilling holes into rock, placing explosives, [music] running steam shovels, and hauling away debris on railroad cars. The operation consumed roughly 400,000 lb [music] of dynamite every single month. That is 200 metric tons of [music] explosive month after month after month. Twice a day, work stopped entirely so that crews could detonate more than 600 dynamite charges at once, blasting apart the mountain side so that steam shovels could scoop [music] up the rubble. By the time the canal was finished in 1914, workers had used over 60 million pounds of dynamite and excavated more than 240 million cubic yards of earth. That is enough dirt to fill more than 17 million dump trucks. The human cost was enormous. At least 25,000 workers died during the construction of the Panama Canal across both the failed French attempt and the American effort that finished it. Dynamite itself claimed many of those lives. Premature detonations, [music] unexloded charges triggered by excavating machines, and workers partially deafened by quinine who could not hear warning signals. All of these contributed to a death toll that would be unthinkable by modern [music] standards. In December of 1908, a single accidental detonation at the Kbra cut killed 23 men at once. And yet without dynamite, [music] the Panama Canal simply could not have been built. There was no alternative explosive available that could have moved that much rock in that amount of time. The canal opened in 1914 and immediately became one of the most important shipping lanes on Earth, connecting 160 countries and 1,700 ports. Every container ship, every oil tanker, every naval vessel that passes through the Panama Canal today is traveling through a channel that was carved by dynamite. The Panama Canal was the headline, but dynamite was quietly [music] transforming every corner of the globe. Mining operations in South Africa, Australia, and the American West used dynamite [music] to extract gold, copper, coal, and diamonds from deep underground. Entire regional economies were built on what dynamite could pull out of the earth. The California gold rush had relied on crude blasting techniques, but the hard rock mining operations that followed used dynamite to go deeper and extract more efficiently than anyone had imagined possible. In Europe, dynamite blasted tunnels through the Alps that connected nations and made overland trade routes possible across terrain that had been impossible for all of human [music] history. The Godard rail tunnel in Switzerland, the roads and rail lines threading through the mountains of Austria and Italy, all of them owed their existence to Nobel's invention. Harbors were deepened, river channels widened, [music] and foundations for bridges laid in bedrock that no previous technology could have touched. The very infrastructure of the modern industrial world, the highways you drive on, the tunnels your trains pass through, the ports [music] where goods arrive from across the ocean, so much of it traces back to sticks of dynamite [music] packed into holes drilled in stone. Think about that for a second. A single invention created by one man in a laboratory outside Stockholm physically reshaped the surface of the planet. [music] Mountains were moved. Continents were connected. Resources buried under miles of rock were [music] brought to the surface and turned into the raw materials of modern civilization. Without dynamite, the modern world as we know it would look fundamentally different. And it would have taken decades [music] longer to build. But Alfred Nobel was about to learn a lesson that every inventor eventually faces. You can control what you create, but you cannot control what people do with it. Just 3 years after dynamite was patented, it was used in combat for the first time. The FrancoRussian [music] War broke out in 1870, and both the French and Prussian armies quickly realized that dynamite could breach fortified positions, destroy defensive walls, and demolish bridges [music] in ways that gunpowder never could. Military engineers on both sides packed dynamite into trenches and tunnels [music] beneath enemy fortifications, detonating charges that collapsed entire defensive lines. The war lasted less than a year, but it gave the world a preview of what industrialized explosives could do on the battlefield. What followed was worse. After France's defeat, the Paris Commune rose up in 1871, and the Communards used dynamite to destroy public monuments and buildings across the city. The French government's forces used it right back. Dynamite had crossed a line. It was no longer just a construction tool. It was now a weapon available to anyone who could get their hands on it. And in the late 19th century, getting your hands on dynamite was not particularly difficult. The group that embraced dynamite most [music] enthusiastically was the anarchist movement. Throughout the 1880s and 1890s, anarchists [music] across Europe carried out a campaign of bombings and assassinations that became known as propaganda by the deed. The idea was [music] simple and terrifying. If you could not overthrow the state through politics or organized labor, you could strike fear into the ruling class [music] with sudden spectacular acts of violence. And dynamite made that possible in a way that no previous weapon had. Before Nobel's invention, explosive capability had been limited to professional armies and state militaries. Dynamite put that same destructive force into the hands of individuals, of small groups operating in secret, of anyone [music] with a grudge and a plan. Bomb-making instructions circulated openly in radical newspapers and pamphlets throughout Europe and the United States. By the mid 1880s, anarchist bombings were shaking cities from London to Barcelona to Chicago. Police raids on anarchist hideouts [music] turned up dynamite, weapons, and instruction manuals with alarming regularity. The violence escalated into what historians have called a decade of reicide. [music] In the 1890s, anarchists assassinated the president of France, the empress of Austria, the king [music] of Italy, and the prime minister of Spain. In 1901, an anarchist named Leon [music] Cholgosh shot and killed American President William McKinley. These were not military operations or organized rebellions. They were acts carried out by [music] individuals, often loners, armed with weapons that would have been unthinkable a generation earlier. Dynamite had democratized destruction [music] and the consequences were being felt at the highest levels of political power around the world. Alfred Nobel watched all of this unfold and it ate at him. He had always believed that the sheer destructive potential of modern explosives would serve as a deterrent to war. In 1891, he wrote that perhaps his factories would put an end to war entirely, reasoning that on the day two armies could annihilate each other in a single second, all civilized nations would recoil in horror and disband their troops. It was a hopeful theory. It was also completely wrong. Governments did not recoil. They ordered more [music] dynamite. Anarchists did not seek peace. They sought spectacle. Nobel himself was a complicated man. He was shy, often ill, and deeply lonely. He never married, and had no children. [music] He loved poetry and literature and had written plays in his younger years. He was not the cold-hearted arms dealer that the newspapers made him out to be, but he was also a businessman who understood exactly what his products [music] were being used for. And the gap between his intentions and the reality of Dynamite's impact grew wider with [music] every passing year. By the late 1880s, Nobel had amassed an enormous fortune. He owned factories on multiple continents. He held hundreds of patents. He had purchased the Bowfor's Iron Works in Sweden, a company he [music] transformed into a major manufacturer of cannons and armaments. He was, whether he liked it or not, one of the most prominent figures in the global weapons industry. And then came the morning in 1888 when everything changed. Nobel's older brother, Ludvig, died while vacationing in K, France. A French newspaper got the [music] brothers confused and published an obituary for Alfred instead. The headline reportedly read, "The merchant of death is dead." The article said that Alfred Nobel had become rich by finding ways to kill more people faster than ever before. Now, historians have debated the exact details of this obituary. Some versions may be embellished, and some scholars question whether the newspaper's language was quite as dramatic as later accounts [music] suggest. What is well documented is that an actual obituary appeared on the front page of the French newspaper Lef Figaro on April 15th, 1888, stating that a man who could only with the utmost difficulty be considered a benefactor of mankind had died. It was retracted the next day when they realized [music] Alfred was still alive. Whether the language was exactly as legend tells it or slightly less theatrical, the impact on Nobel was [music] real. He was shaken. He was confronted with the undeniable fact that the world saw [music] him not as an inventor who had advanced civilization, but as a propheteer who had made killing easier. And he decided [music] in that moment, or in the months that followed, that he was not going to let that be the final word on his life. Nobel spent the next several years quietly restructuring his affairs. On November 27th, 1895, at [music] the Swedish Norwegian Club in Paris, he signed his last will and testament. The document was unlike anything [music] anyone expected. Nobel directed that after taxes and personal bequests, 94% of [music] his total assets, a sum of 31,225,000 Swedish crona, be set aside to establish a fund. That fund would award annual [music] prizes to individuals who had, in his words, conferred the greatest benefit to humankind. The prizes would be [music] given in five categories: physics, chemistry, medicine or physiology, literature, and peace. The peace prize [music] is the one that tells you everything. A man who had spent his life building explosives, who owned cannon factories [music] and held patents on military propellants, specifically created a prize for the person or organization that had [music] done the most to promote peace and disarmament. His close friendship with the Austrian [music] pacifist and author Bertha von Sutner had clearly influenced him. Von Sutner had been his secretary for a brief period and the two corresponded for decades [music] afterward. She was one of the most vocal peace activists in Europe and there is strong reason to believe that her influence was the driving force behind the peace prize specifically. Nobel never publicly [music] discussed why he created the prizes. He left no diary entry, no letter explaining his thinking, but the timing [music] coming just 7 years after he read his own obituary tells a story of its own. [music] The man who the world called the merchant of death was determined to be remembered differently. Alfred Nobel died on December 10th, 1896 at his villa in San Remo, Italy. He was 63 years old. He died of a cerebral hemorrhage alone far from Sweden [music] in a country where he had lived out his final years partly because he despised the Nordic winters. When his will was read, his family was stunned. So were the governments of Sweden and Norway, who were now tasked with administering a [music] prize fund worth the equivalent of roughly 250 million modern American dollars. It took several years of legal disputes and administrative [music] wrangling before the Nobel Foundation was formally established. But in 1901, the first Nobel Prizes were awarded. Today, the Nobel Prize is arguably the most prestigious honor a human being can receive. Nobel laureates include Albert Einstein, [music] Marie Cury, Martin Luther King Jr. and dozens of other figures who reshaped science, literature, and the [music] cause of peace. The synthetic element Nobelium was named after Alfred Noble. Companies descended from his business ventures still operate around the world. His name echoes through [music] history, and when most people hear it, they think of the prizes, not the explosives. That is one of the strangest [music] legacies in the history of invention. The man who gave the world its most destructive civilian tool also gave it [music] the most respected award for advancing human knowledge and promoting peace. Dynamite carved the Panama Canal, blasted open gold mines, and punched tunnels through mountain ranges that had blocked trade and travel for centuries. It also [music] armed anarchists, fueled wars, and turned its creator into a figure associated with death and destruction. The same sticks of explosive that built the railroads connecting the American continent were used [music] to blow apart fortifications and assassinate heads of state across Europe. And that duality has never really gone away. Dynamite is still used in construction [music] and mining operations around the world today. Every time you drive through a highway [music] tunnel, every time a ship passes through the Panama Canal, every time a minor descends into a shaft blasted out of solid rock, the fingerprints of Alfred Nobel's invention are there. The phone in your pocket [music] contains minerals extracted from mines that were opened with dynamite. Dynamite is embedded so deeply into the physical infrastructure of [music] modern life that we do not even notice it anymore. Alfred Nobel wanted to make the world safer. He watched nitroglycerin kill workers, kill his own brother, and terrorize communities. And he dedicated his life to taming that substance into something controllable. He succeeded. Dynamite saved countless lives in mining and construction [music] by replacing far more dangerous explosives. But the same invention that saved those lives also took thousands of others in wars and acts of terrorism that Nobel never anticipated. He spent his final years grappling with that contradiction. And the [music] Nobel Prizes are his answer to it. Not an apology exactly, more like a bet. A bet that humanity could use knowledge and creativity and the pursuit of peace to outweigh the destruction that his invention had made possible.
